newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek minister to meet farmers mounting blockade.
newsitem.headline: Greek minister to meet farmers mounting blockade.

text.p: Greece's agriculture chief will on Wednesday talk to leaders of thousands of angry farmers blockading national roads and railways soon after a meeting of ministers chaired by Prime Minister Costas Simitis.

Officials said Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas will travel to the central town of Larissa, the centre of the farmers' protests, where thousands of tractors have blocked the road linking Athens and the northern port of Salonika, Greece's second-largest city.
The week-long blockade has caused transport chaos throughout Greece but the farmers have vowed to continue their action over Christmas to press demands for better prices and cheaper fuel.

"Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas will meet the farmers on Wednesday after a government meeting chaired by the prime minister," Thanasis Papageorgiou, the vice-governor of the state Agricultural Bank of Greece, told reporters.

Vangelis Boutas, a farmers' representative, said: "We hope Mr Tzoumakas will come up in Larissa with some constructive proposals. If he comes up with just promises then the roadblocks will continue for as long as it takes."

The blockade has caused chaos at more than 40 spots on the national road network with farmers brushing off government pleas to end the protest and warnings that they are inflicting heavy damage on Grece's economy.
"We understand the farmers' problems but they must realise that the blockade will have a dramatic effect on the economy if they continue," Papageorgiou said.

The protest, deploying some 10,000 tractors, is to press demands for lower fuel prices, lower Value Added Tax (VAT) on equipment, higher farm subsides and the rescheduling of some $1.3 billion in farmers' debts with state banks.

Queues of trapped international and domestic lorries are growing longer by the day. Hundreds of trucks could be seen stretching along highways while others tried to inch their way along narrow country lanes to skirt the barricades.

"We've been here for three days with no food, no water, no toilets," a driver told reporters at the western port of Patras on Tuesday. He was carrying a cargo from Germany to a NATO base on the island of Crete.
Bus passengers travelling from Patras to Athens had to get off one bus, walk for about 200 metres (yards) with their luggage through the barricades and then get on another bus to continue their trip.
Bonfires of tyres lit up the night. Despite bitter cold and rain, farmers have set up sprawling motorway camps with chairs, tables and plastic tent shelters.
A similar protest in 1995 lasted 10 days, sent food prices soaring and cost the economy tens of millions of dollars but the farmers seemed in a festive mood and unconcerned about economic damage.
"We're farmers. We work the fields. That's our job. Farmers can't go to Brussels to protest for their rights. That's the goverment's job," Dimitris Paskos told Reuters Television.
The government has said its hands are tied by European Union regulations which ban member states from subsidising produce prices.
"Intransigence does not benefit the farmers' problems or the country," said government spokesman Yannis Nikolaou. "Everyone must understand that the situation must not and cannot continue."
